issue.title: perf(opensearch): preload search files on new self-hosted indexes
issue.body: ## Description After an OpenSearch restart, search on a large single-shard index is very slow until the page cache fills. Each search reads its own part of the vectors and HNSW graph with thousands of small random reads. On the eRAG benchmark box (1.56M chunks, Cohere v3 1024-dim, 17.9 GB index, gp3 disk), the first searches took about 18 s each, it took about 400 searches (10 to 12 minutes) to settle, and concurrent chat questions in the first minutes hit the 60 s OpenSearch timeout and were answered without documents. This PR sets `index.store.preload` on new self-hosted indexes. When a shard opens, OpenSearch reads the listed files into memory in one sequential pass: - `vec` (float32 vectors) on an unquantized index, or `veq` (quantized vectors) on a 7-bit or 1-bit index. A quantized index reads `.vec` only to rescore its top candidates, so preloading `.vec` would undo the memory saving. - `vex` (HNSW graph), `doc` (postings), `tim`/`tip` (terms), `dvd` (doc values), `cfs` (compound files of small segments). - Stored text (`fdt`), positions and payloads are not listed. The default `hybridfs` store reads them without memory mapping, so preload cannot apply to them, and only the top hits read text (#17288). AWS managed indexes do not set it: they are multi-shard, and the multi-tenant index is far larger than node memory. The setting applies only when an index is created, so existing indexes keep their current behavior until they are reindexed. The OpenSearch deployment guide (`documentation/deployment/local/opensearch.mdx`) has a new "Startup after a restart" section with the longer startup, the new-index-only scope, the AWS exclusion and the memory need. ## How Has This Been Tested? - New external dependency test `test_store_preload.py`: creates indexes through `verify_and_create_index_if_necessary` for none, 7-bit and 1-bit quantization and checks the preload list that OpenSearch stores. A second test checks that AWS managed settings have no preload. - `tests/external_dependency_unit/opensearch/test_opensearch_client.py` and the OpenSearch document index tests pass locally. - Manual test on the eRAG benchmark box (OpenSearch 3.6), same preload list set on the existing 1.56M-chunk index, cold restart (OpenSearch stopped, page cache dropped, started), then 100 searches in a row: | Cold restart | No preload | Preload | |---|---|---| | Time until the index is ready | ~30 s | 149 s | | Data in page cache when ready | ~0 GB | 15 GB | | First search | 18.1 s | 1.1 s | | Median, searches 1 to 10 | 18.1 s | 504 ms | | Median, searches 51 to 100 | 1.6 s | 408 ms (warm: 403 ms) | | Total, first 100 searches | 526 s | 43 s | The trade is about two more minutes before the index can serve search, in place of about ten minutes of slow searches and timeouts. A new index without the legacy title vectors would preload about 8.5 GB instead of 15 GB. ## Additional Options - [ ] [Optional] Please cherry-pick this PR to the latest release version. - [ ] [Optional] Override Linear Check --- ## Summary by cubic Sets `index.store.preload` on new self-hosted OpenSearch indexes so shard-open reads the vectors, HNSW graph, postings, terms, doc values, and compound files into memory in one sequential pass. Previously each search after a restart waited on thousands of random disk reads, keeping search slow for roughly ten minutes and risking 60s timeouts; now the index takes about two minutes longer to become ready but serves search in ~500ms immediately. - Quantized indexes preload the quantized vectors (`veq`) instead of the float32 copy (`vec`), preserving the memory saving. - AWS managed indexes do not set the setting; they are multi-shard and sized by AWS. - The setting applies only when an index is created, so existing indexes keep current behavior until reindexed. - The local deployment docs explain the longer startup, the new-index-only scope, and the memory needed to hold the preloaded files. Preloading reduces cold reads; it is not a guarantee, because OpenSearch may evict files from memory if memory is too small. Written for commit 087368f0658989f7f40b92d7427aa8b96a870b4f. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * Newly created self-hosted indexes preload selected vector, graph, and keyword files. Quantized indexes preload the matching quantized vector files; stored text and AWS-managed indexes are excluded. * Preloading applies only when an index is created. After a restart, searches wait for these files to load into memory, which may increase startup time depending on file size and disk speed. * Preloading requires enough memory to retain the files.

comment.body:
Re the outside-diff CodeRabbit comment on `schema.py` (wait for the primary shard before reporting ready): not changing this.

- API readiness cannot cover the case. An OpenSearch restart alone does not restart the API server, so a startup gate in the API would never run for it.
- The window is not new. Without preload, the shard is also unavailable while it starts (about 30 s on the eRAG box), and then searches run 10 to 30 s each for minutes, with 60 s timeouts. With preload, the unavailable window is longer (about 2.5 min for 15 GB) and searches fail fast during it, then run at near-warm speed.
- When the API and OpenSearch start together, blocking API startup on the shard would only delay the API; it would not let searches succeed sooner.

The OpenSearch deployment guide now says that searches return an error until the preload completes.

issue.title: docs(resourcing): add an OpenSearch sizing calculator
issue.body: ## Description Adds an interactive OpenSearch sizing calculator to the Resourcing page (`snippets/opensearch-sizing-calculator.jsx`). Step 1 turns total storage and a storage mix into chunks, index size and vector memory for the chosen embedding model and quantization. Step 2 recommends data nodes, memory and storage per node, primary shards and replicas, and names the limit that sets the node count. The scaling section becomes "OpenSearch Sizing": the source-data storage formula, per-GB scaling guidelines and old example are replaced by what drives storage, when to scale, and a worked example; the heap guidance is corrected to at most 31 GB with where Compose and Helm set it. ## How Has This Been Tested? Rendered in `mint dev` (light and dark, desktop and phone width) and exercised every control; the example table matches the calculator's output and an independent recomputation of its formulas. `format_docs.py --check` passes. Defaults (Granite 384 dims, no quantization, 1 replica) match `main`. The per-chunk and text-per-GB values are estimates from a benchmark corpus and are labelled as such on the page. ## Additional Options - [ ] [Optional] Please cherry-pick this PR to the latest release version. - [ ] [Optional] Override Linear Check --- ## Summary by cubic Adds an interactive OpenSearch sizing calculator to the Resourcing page. The calculator turns total storage, a storage mix, growth, embedding model, and quantization into chunk counts, index size, and vector memory, then recommends data nodes, memory and storage per node, primary shards, and replicas. The scaling section becomes "OpenSearch Sizing": the source-data storage formula, per-GB scaling guidelines, and old example are replaced by what drives storage, when to scale, and a worked example; heap guidance is corrected to at most 31 GB with where Docker Compose and Helm set it. Per-file text estimates are retitled, and per-chunk values are labeled as estimates from a benchmark corpus. **Details** - Chunks are sized for the released Onyx (5.1) index format at about 2,650 bytes fixed; a later release drops the stored text copy and title vector, roughly halving that until a reindex. - Shard counts are chosen so copies divide evenly over nodes; example rows list the exact `OPENSEARCH_INDEX_NUM_SHARDS` and `OPENSEARCH_INDEX_NUM_REPLICAS` settings. - The storage input is clamped to 10,000,000 GB and the shard math is bounded so huge or non-finite inputs cannot freeze the page; a typed value above the cap changes the field to show the capped value. - Notes that 1-bit quantization requires OpenSearch 3.6 or later and shrinks the vectors, not the graph links. Written for commit 7058a4581df8841c3caf41c6e189a3a3c9bf63f8. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * Added an interactive OpenSearch sizing calculator that estimates chunk counts, storage, vector-search memory, node count, and primary shards using configurable storage, growth, embedding, quantization, and copy settings. * The calculator recommends node and cluster settings, accounts for availability zones, and highlights capacity guidance. * **Documentation** * Replaced general resource-scaling guidance with an OpenSearch sizing guide covering memory, storage, JVM and disk thresholds, scaling actions, and deployment examples. * Clarified that shard-count changes require a new index, while replica counts can be changed on an existing index.

comment.body: On the follow-up about using `1.1 * (dimension * bits_per_dimension / 8 + 8 * m)` for vector-search memory: keeping the current model. That formula estimates the in-memory graph of OpenSearch's native k-NN engines (faiss, nmslib), which load graphs into the plugin's native memory. Onyx maps its vector field with the Lucene engine, which keeps the HNSW graph in compressed files (`.vex`) read through the OS file cache. On our 1.56M-chunk benchmark indexes those files measured about 40 bytes per chunk per vector field, against the formula's 8 × 32 = 256 bytes. So the calculator uses the vector bytes plus the measured ~40 bytes, and it already counts only 80% of each node's file cache for vectors as headroom.

issue.title: feat(opensearch): default AWS to 3.7 and disable quantization levels the cluster cannot index
issue.body: ## Description 1-bit vector quantization needs OpenSearch 3.6 or later. This PR makes that visible in two places. **Terraform.** The AWS `opensearch` module and the `onyx` wrapper both defaulted to OpenSearch 3.3, so domains created from them could not use 1-bit. Both defaults are now 3.7. Amazon OpenSearch Service offers 3.1, 3.3, 3.5 and 3.7 (checked with `aws opensearch list-versions` in us-east-2 and us-west-2), so 3.7 is the first offered version with 1-bit. A domain that relies on the default upgrades in place on its next `terraform apply`. Domains that set `opensearch_engine_version` are not affected. The Terraform guide now documents the input, the upgrade on apply, how to keep the current version, and to confirm 3.7 with `aws opensearch list-versions` first. **Index Settings.** Before, choosing 1-bit on an older cluster failed only after **Apply & Re-index**. A new endpoint, `GET /search-settings/vector-quantization-support`, returns the cluster's OpenSearch version and which quantization levels it can index, using the same rule as the reindex validator. Index Settings shows an unsupported level as disabled, with "Needs OpenSearch 3.6+" and a tooltip naming the cluster's version. An unknown version, a failed request, or Onyx Cloud restricts nothing. The server-side check is unchanged. ## How Has This Been Tested? - External dependency tests (`test_vector_quantization_support.py`): against the local 3.6 cluster every level is supported; with the version stubbed to 3.3, 1-bit is unsupported, 7-bit is supported, and the validator agrees; with no reported version nothing is restricted. - Existing search-settings unit tests pass (425). - Playwright: a stubbed 3.3 cluster shows 1-bit disabled with its note and 7-bit selectable. - Local stack on images from this branch: the endpoint reports 3.6 with all levels supported, 3.3 (stubbed) with 1-bit unsupported, and 403 without a login. - OpenSearch 3.7 (local container): the document index, reindex port and port-flow end-to-end suites pass (both MODEL_ONLY and COPY_VECTORS), including 1-bit and 7-bit quantization and the new endpoint. - Fixed `test_port_flow_e2e.py`: its MODEL_ONLY case relied on `ASYM_PASSAGE_PREFIX`, which is now empty for the default encoder, so it compared equal prefixes. It now sets nomic's prefixes explicitly. CI skips this test (needs a model server). - `terraform fmt`, the docs formatter, and pre-commit pass. ## Additional Options - [ ] [Optional] Please cherry-pick this PR to the latest release version. - [x] [Optional] Override Linear Check ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * Vector quantization settings show which options are supported by your OpenSearch cluster. Options requiring a newer version are disabled and display the minimum required version. * **Updates** * The default OpenSearch engine version is now 3.7. 1-bit vector quantization requires OpenSearch 3.6 or later. * **Documentation** * Documented the engine-version setting, its default, and how to check regional availability. Applying Terraform without specifying a version may upgrade an existing domain to 3.7; specify its current version to avoid that upgrade.

The DECISION default is the same value the Decision Models page shows. Search Mode and Auto-Detect Search Filters move into the first card. **Gate** (`SearchTool._resolve_decision_client`, once per search call). The new path runs only when: - a default decision model is configured, - the turn persists content (the decision client carries no incognito request policy, so content-free turns keep LLM selection), and - on cloud (PostHog available), the flag `onyx-search-decision-rerank-expansion` is on for the tenant. Self-hosted needs only the configured model. There is no env var. **Decision path** (`search_tool.py`, new `secondary_llm_flows/decision_rerank_expansion.py`, questions in `prompts/search_prompts.py`): 1. Take the first 100 fused sections and trim them to 4× the selection token budget. 2. Rank them in one decision request with one comparative yes/no question per section. Predicate probabilities are comparable only within one request, so the sections are never split. 3. Keep the 10 most probable sections. Equal probabilities keep fusion order. Picks beyond the top hits get search docs. 4. Expand the first 10 fused sections in the background while the ranking call runs; search waits only for the selected ones. Jest: 24 passed in the changed suites. - The benchmark used the same path on an experiment branch. This branch has not run against a live stack yet. ## Docs - [x] Customer-facing change: I updated `documentation/` (text and screenshots). - [ ] No docs change needed (internal, tests, CI, or multi-tenant cloud only). `admins/managing_features/chat.mdx` (Search Decision Model, moved switches, both Chat Preferences screenshots recaptured), `admins/managing_features/rag_and_search.mdx` and `admins/ai_models/overview.mdx`. The Decision Models page no longer says "Onyx does not use this model yet". ## Additional Options - [ ] [Optional] Please cherry-pick this PR to the latest release version. > [!NOTE] > > > [!NOTE] > ### Add decision-model reranking and context expansion to internal search > - Internal search can now rank sections with a decision model instead of LLM section selection. `SearchTool._select_with_decision_model` ranks up to 100 candidate sections in a single listwise decision request (5s timeout), picks the top 10, and keeps fusion order for ties. See [search_tool.py](https://github.com/onyx-dot-app/onyx/pull/16919/files#diff-af40a8152b9ef8757efde2e088361bb59c6fdb7aa1338e98d42a3656f916da0a) and [decision_rerank_expansion.py](https://github.com/onyx-dot-app/onyx/pull/16919/files#diff-1068fb819eaff8004166a77f8a894dd4641182cc97257615492318c0244f4bb4). > - Selected sections can be context-expanded with the decision model via [search_utils.py](https://github.com/onyx-dot-app/onyx/pull/16919/files#diff-f784aaba06a68abf783a75af5119a7e3c54e89d2a8636198f9b668b55d96a12c).
